old: He whose disease arises with all its causes, premonitory signs (prāgrūpa) and signs (rūpa), each in its own way, to excess; or a sick man in whom quickly there are, on the face, moles (piplu, probably), blemishes (vyaṅga, probably), lines (lekhā) and tilakālaka (black specks of the skin, probably), or, on the nails and teeth, flowers (puṣpa), or, on the belly, veins (sirā) of various colours; he who, while wasting away, has a coating on the eyes (netra-upadeha), a swelling of either the eyelid or the nose, or a drooping of the eyelid; he who, being wasted, has hunger or thirst that is not allayed even by many agreeable foods and drinks; he from whom frothy blood is discharged, with pain in the flank and (pain) of the chest, or; he whose phlegm (śleṣman) is blue, yellow and red, and repeatedly so; he who has a strong crushing of the neck, dryness of the tongue, and inflammation (pāka, literally 'ripening') of the throat, mouth and anus; he who has parikartikā (cutting pain) arising in the āmāśaya (probably the stomach), excessive thirst and breaking of the stool; he who has parikartikā arising in the pakvāśaya (probably the large intestine), excessive thirst and an excessive grasp of the anus (gudagraha); he in whom wind (vāyu), having resorted to either the āmāśaya or the pakvāśaya and having destroyed consciousness (saṃjñā), makes a gurgling sound (ghurghuraka) in the throat; he who, wasted, has increase of thirst and pain in the heart, and likewise hiccup and bloody diarrhoea, or bloating and diarrhoea, and who is greatly thirsty: he is parāsu (one whose life-breaths are gone).

old: One long prose sentence of alternative signs, each introduced by 'yasya' ('of whom/whose'); the closing 'sa parāsuḥ iti' gives the conclusion for each. Copula understood in the verbless clauses (shown as 'has' or 'there are'). The closing 'iti' is not translated. 'parāsu' = one whose life-breaths (asu) have gone; the line itself does not say 'doomed to die', so no more is added (the chapter appears to list fatal signs, but that is not stated here). Printed 'vāyasyāśu' = vā yasya āśu; 'cauraso' = ca urasaḥ (hiatus printed joined; 'śūla' of the chest is understood from kukṣiśūlam). 'puṣpa' = flowers, read literally; later medicine uses it for white spots on the nails (not adopted). tilakālaka, piplu and vyaṅga are skin marks (probable identifications). 'bahuśaḥ' is read as 'repeatedly'. 'netropadeha' = coating (smearing) on the eyes. 'śakṛdbheda' = breaking of the stool (probably loose stool). 'gudagraha' = grasp of the anus. 'āmapakvāśayānyataram' is read as 'one of the two, āmāśaya or pakvāśaya'. 'hidhmā-raktātisārau' and 'ādhmāna-atīsārau' are dual dvandvas (two members each). The avagraha printed after -ā (parikartikā'ti-) is a print habit. 'kṣaṇisya' is read as kṣīṇasya (flagged).
